newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seeks spot among Europe leaders in NATO vote.
newsitem.headline: Spain seeks spot among Europe leaders in NATO vote.

text.p: Spain should take a more active role in NATO to secure its place among the leading nations of Europe, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar said on Wednesday.

Aznar was speaking at a two-day parliamentary debate on Spain's full integration into NATO's military structure. The government's resolution, supported by the main opposition party, should pass easily in a vote set for Thursday.
"(Spain) has the opportunity to consolidate its position among the largest European nations," Aznar said.

Spain does not want to be left behind the first tier of European countries, whether it be in NATO as the alliance looks to expand eastward or in the drive to form a European economic and monetary union.
The vote on Thursday will cement Spain's ambivalent relationship with the 16-member alliance over the years.

Under former Socialist prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, Spain joined NATO in 1982 but froze integration into the military wing pending a referendum on continued membership. The 1986 referendum passed with 52 percent of voters saying "yes".
But Spaniards' support came with a few strings attached.

The government promised in return a reduction in U.S. troops stationed in Spain which then numbered 12,500. The country was to remain free of nuclear weapons. And Gonzalez vowed Spain would stay outside NATO's military command structure.

Aznar, who took office in May after 13 years of Socialist rule, says circumstances have been transformed beyond recognition by the end of the Cold War and by the alliance's decision this year to allow European allies to use NATO equipment and resources for their own operations.

In talks with NATO about integration into the new command structure, Spain is demanding it host a sub-regional command on its territory controlling all of the Iberian peninsula including access to the Mediterranean through the Straits of Gibraltar.
"It is unthinkable that Spain will not have a sub-regional command on its territory," Gonzalez said in the debate on Wednesday.

The government has pledged that Spain remain free of nuclear weapons. In 1986, the government saw its relationship with NATO as the key to closer ties with western Europe at a time Spain when was trying to shed decades of isolation.
The referendum came just three months after Spain had joined the European Community and Gonzalez said then the country could not shirk its responsibilities for European defence.

This time around, the deepening of ties with NATO takes place against the backdrop of Spanish efforts to discipline its economy so it can qualify for the founding group of states in a European economic and monetary union in 1999.
Spain will take on its new role in NATO at a time when the organisation is looking to cast its net wider to include former Warsaw Pact countries, an expansion supported by Spain.
The main holdout in parliament against full intergration is communist Julio Anguita's pacifistic United Left coalition.

Traditional opposition in Spain to joining NATO's military structure came from a coalition of trade unions, pacifists, artists, ecologists and far left groups who feared nuclear war and were hostile to the United States for its support of the late Spanish dictator General Francisco Franco.
But the proponents of full integration have tried to allay those fears by stressing NATO's increasing role in peacekeeping.
